name: Guanyin Bodhisattva
domain: Great Compassion, Rescue from Suffering, Hearing the Cries of the World
description: Whatever you believe, chances are that at the hardest moment of your life you have whispered 'Guanyin Ma, protect me.' Guanyin Bodhisattva (Guanshiyin), affectionately called Guanyin Ma or Guanyin Fozu in Taiwan, is the white-robed figure holding a vase of pure water and a willow branch, the most approachable bodhisattva of all, honored across Buddhism, Taoism, and folk belief alike. Her work comes down to one phrase: rescuing those who suffer. The sutras say she has thirty-two forms and goes wherever there is pain, no matter your faith and no matter what you have done. Curiously, Guanyin was originally depicted as male in Indian Buddhism. After reaching China, the image gradually became feminine from around the Northern and Southern Dynasties, and by the Tang and Song it had settled into the white-robed, motherly figure we know today. Some scholars say that is because, to the Chinese heart, the highest form of compassion is a mother's love. Walk into almost any temple in Taiwan, whoever the main deity is, and you will most likely find Guanyin somewhere inside.
story:
What moves people most about Guanyin is that she never gives up. Legend says she had long since earned the right to become a Buddha, yet she made a vow: as long as any being is still suffering, she will not take her place among the Buddhas but will stay in the world to help. This is what 'hearing the cries and coming to save' means: the moment someone calls, she is on her way.

People in Taiwan are especially fond of a modern version. A man falls into the sea and shouts with all his strength, 'Guanyin, save me!' A boat comes, and he refuses to climb in. A helicopter comes, and he still refuses, certain the bodhisattva herself will appear. He drowns, and afterward he asks her, 'I called so loudly. Why didn't you save me?' Guanyin answers, 'The boat and the helicopter were both sent by me.'

Folk wisdom uses this story as a gentle reminder: a bodhisattva's help often hides in the chance right in front of you, and whether a prayer 'works' also depends on whether you are willing to reach out and take it.

temples.name: Manka Longshan Temple
temples.deityStory: Manka Longshan Temple, dedicated mainly to Guanyin Bodhisattva, is Taipei's most famous historic temple. When the Taipei Air Raid of 1945 destroyed its main hall, the Guanyin statue survived, which devotees took as a sign of the bodhisattva's divine presence.

temples.name: Linkou Zhulinshan Guanyin Temple
temples.deityStory: Home to an Eighteen-Armed Guanyin and always busy with worshippers, this temple is the center of faith for the Linkou and Taoyuan area. Its buildings are grand and its gardens beautifully landscaped.

associatedTemples: Manka Longshan Temple (Wanhua District, Taipei City)
Linkou Zhulinshan Guanyin Temple (Linkou District, New Taipei City)
Qingshui Ziyun Temple (Qingshui District, Taichung City)
Neimen Zizhu Temple (Neimen District, Kaohsiung City)
worship: What do people ask Guanyin for? Safety and health, protection from misfortune, the wellbeing of their children. But what she does best is bring peace of mind, and she feels especially close when something weighs on your heart that you cannot get past. Praying to her is simple: offer fresh flowers, fruit, and clear tea, put your palms together, silently recite 'Namo Guanshiyin Pusa' three times, then lay out your troubles slowly, the way you would talk to an elder. The simpler the offering, the better; Guanyin does not care for show. There is just one taboo you must never forget: Guanyin is vegetarian, so no meat may be offered. Putting chicken, duck, fish, or pork on her altar is a serious act of disrespect. Around Guanyin's birthday on the 19th day of the second lunar month, Guanyin temples such as Longshan Temple are at their busiest, so that is the time to go if you want to feel the atmosphere.
festivals: Guanyin has three major commemorative days: her birthday on the 19th day of the second lunar month, the day of her enlightenment on the 19th day of the sixth lunar month, and the day she renounced the world on the 19th day of the ninth lunar month. On each of these days, temples hold sutra-chanting services to pray for blessings. The birthday on the 19th of the second month is the grandest of the three, when incense burns especially thick at Buddhist temples across Taiwan and in the Guanyin halls of folk Mazu temples.

name: Shakyamuni Buddha
domain: Founder of Buddhism, Teacher of the Three Realms, Symbol of Compassion and Wisdom
description: On a moonlit night some 2,500 years ago, a prince mounted a white horse, slipped away from his sleeping wife and child, and never looked back. He was Shakyamuni Buddha, known in Taiwan as Fozu, the World-Honored One, or Rulai Buddha: the founder of Buddhism, born Siddhartha Gautama into the royal family of Kapilavastu in ancient India. At 29, on what are called the 'four excursions' beyond the palace gates, he came face to face with old age, sickness, and death, and resolved to leave home in search of liberation. He finally attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree. In Taiwan, the four great Buddhist communities, Fo Guang Shan, Dharma Drum Mountain, Tzu Chi, and Chung Tai Chan Monastery, each have their own style, yet all honor Shakyamuni as their root teacher. A quick way to tell three figures apart: Shakyamuni is the teacher who really lived in this world, Amitabha is the Buddha of the Western Pure Land, and Guanyin is a bodhisattva who has not yet become a Buddha. Get these three straight before you step into a Buddhist temple, and you will pay your respects with more confidence.
story:
Legend says that Prince Siddhartha took seven steps the moment he was born, and a lotus bloomed under each one. But the real story begins outside the palace walls. On the day of the four excursions he saw a stooped old man, a groaning sick man, a cold, stiff corpse, and finally a wandering ascetic with a settled gaze, and in an instant wealth and luxury lost all their weight. On a moonlit night at 29, he rode out on his white horse Kanthaka, accompanied by his attendant Channa, and left the city to become a renunciant. Six years of harsh austerities followed, until, starved to skin and bone, he understood that tormenting the body would not buy awakening.

On the banks of the Nairanjana River he accepted an offering of milk-rice from the shepherdess Sujata, regained his strength, and sat down beneath the Bodhi tree, vowing not to rise until he had attained enlightenment. According to legend, the demon king Mara sent his daughters and then his armies to disturb him, and he overcame them all. Before dawn he fully realized dependent origination and the Four Noble Truths, becoming the Buddha, the Awakened One. For more than forty years after that he walked the Ganges basin teaching, with everyone from kings to butchers among his listeners, until at last he passed peacefully into nirvana between twin trees at Kushinagar.

temples.name: Dharma Drum Mountain
temples.deityStory: Dharma Drum Mountain, one of Taiwan's four great Buddhist mountains, was founded by Master Sheng Yen. Its main hall enshrines Shakyamuni Buddha, and it emphasizes 'spiritual environmentalism' and building a pure land on earth, making it an important center of modern Buddhist practice.

temples.name: Fo Guang Shan (Buddha's Light Mountain)
temples.deityStory: Fo Guang Shan was founded by Venerable Master Hsing Yun in 1967. Its Great Hero Hall, majestic and solemn, enshrines Shakyamuni Buddha. Fo Guang Shan is devoted to spreading 'Humanistic Buddhism,' and its influence reaches around the world.

associatedTemples: Dharma Drum Mountain (Jinshan District, New Taipei City)
Fo Guang Shan (Buddha's Light Mountain) (Dashu District, Kaohsiung City)
Chung Tai Chan Monastery (Puli Township, Nantou County)
worship: Worshipping the Buddha calls for no lavish meat dishes; quite the opposite. Offerings are simply incense, fresh flowers, and fruit, all vegetarian, which is the most basic taboo. When paying respects, bring your palms together and make three bows, or perform three kneelings and nine prostrations, silently reciting 'Namo Benshi Shijiamouni Fo' (Homage to our root teacher Shakyamuni Buddha), or chant the Heart Sutra or the Great Compassion Mantra. Buddhism teaches that sincerity is what matters: the simpler the offering the better, because the point is the heart. If you want to pray for blessings, most temples offer guangming lamps you can light. As for where to go: Fo Guang Shan emphasizes Humanistic Buddhism, Dharma Drum Mountain emphasizes meditation, Tzu Chi is known for charity, and Chung Tai Chan Monastery focuses on meditation and education. Each of the four great communities has its own character, so just choose the one that suits you.
festivals:
Shakyamuni Buddha has three important commemorative days in Taiwan, together known as the 'three great Buddhist festivals':

**Buddha's Birthday (Bathing the Buddha Festival)**: the 8th day of the fourth lunar month, **which falls on May 24 in 2026**. Temples hold Bathing the Buddha ceremonies in which devotees pour fragrant water over a small statue of the newborn Buddha, symbolizing washing the dust from one's heart and returning to one's originally pure nature. Tzu Chi combines Buddha's Birthday, Mother's Day, and Tzu Chi Day into a single 'three-in-one' commemoration that emphasizes gratitude and filial devotion to parents.

**The Buddha's Renunciation Day**: the 8th day of the second lunar month, commemorating the night Prince Siddhartha left the city to renounce the world. Temples mostly hold sutra chanting and Dharma talks.

**The Buddha's Enlightenment Day (Laba Festival)**: the 8th day of the twelfth lunar month. Following tradition, temples cook Laba congee, a mix of eight ingredients such as rice, beans, nuts, and lotus seeds, and give it out to devotees, recalling the milk-rice the shepherdess offered the Buddha before his enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.

In addition, the 15th day of the second lunar month is the day of the Buddha's nirvana, and some temples hold memorial services on that day as well.

name: Amitabha Buddha
domain: Guiding Souls to Rebirth, Pure Land Faith, Dissolving Karma and Obstacles
description: In Taiwan, people say 'Amituofo' to greet each other, to say thank you, even to sigh; when a Buddha's name becomes everyday speech, you know how deeply it has spread. Amitabha Buddha, also called the Buddha of Infinite Life, the Buddha of Infinite Light, and the Welcoming Buddha, presides over the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Pure Land practice of reciting the Buddha's name teaches that anyone who sincerely believes, vows, and recites 'Namo Amituofo' will be met by the Buddha at the moment of death and guided to rebirth in the Western Pure Land. No deep learning is required, and anyone can say a single Buddha's name, which is exactly why it has become the most widespread Buddhist practice in Taiwan. From seven-day recitation retreats in temples and daily practice to the chanting machine at an elder's bedside, this name is recited day and night across the island. Together with Guanyin and Mahasthamaprapta (Dashizhi) Bodhisattvas, he forms the 'Three Sages of the West,' and he is what many Taiwanese lean on most when facing life and death.
story:
The Infinite Life Sutra tells of a king, countless eons ago, who was so shaken by hearing the Dharma that he made an astonishing decision: he gave up his entire kingdom to become a monk, taking the name Dharmakara. Before the Buddha Lokesvararaja he made forty-eight great vows, and the eighteenth is the crucial one, the vow that ten recitations are enough: if any being sincerely believes, joyfully wishes to be born in my land, and recites my name even ten times at the end of life, I will surely come to receive them; if this vow is not fulfilled, I will not become a Buddha.

After countless eons of practice, every one of the forty-eight vows was fulfilled, and Dharmakara became a Buddha named Amitabha. The Western Pure Land created by the power of his vows has ground paved with gold, lotuses blooming in pools of the seven treasures, and mandarava flowers drifting down from the sky, and all suffering is gone. A king gave up a kingdom he could see and in return made a pure land that catches every being. That is why, for over a thousand years, so many people have spoken his name in the last moments of their lives.

temples.name: Nung Chan Monastery
temples.deityStory: Nung Chan Monastery was first founded by Elder Master Dongchu; after Master Sheng Yen took it over, it became the birthplace of Dharma Drum Mountain. Its 'Water-Moon Monastery,' designed by architect Kris Yao and completed in 2012, has more than five thousand characters of the Diamond Sutra carved into its walls, reflected in a pool of water. The monastery regularly holds Buddha Seven retreats (seven days of recitation) and meditation activities.

temples.name: Fo Guang Shan (Buddha's Light Mountain)
temples.deityStory: Fo Guang Shan was founded by Venerable Master Hsing Yun. The great welcoming Buddha at the mountain's Great Buddha Land is Amitabha, 120 chi (traditional Chinese feet) tall and completed in 1975. Fo Guang Shan spreads the Dharma through the ideal of 'Humanistic Buddhism,' with facilities such as the Buddha Museum and the Tsung Lin University.

associatedTemples: Nung Chan Monastery (Beitou District, Taipei City)
Fo Guang Shan (Buddha's Light Mountain) (Dashu District, Kaohsiung City)
worship: Offerings to Amitabha are kept simple: fresh flowers, fruit, clear water, and incense, and no meat. The heart of the practice is reciting his name, saying 'Namo Amituofo' over and over, aloud or silently, often counting on prayer beads, until the name is woven into daily life. Many Taiwanese Buddhists chant the Amitabha Sutra as part of their daily practice and dedicate the merit to karmic creditors from past lives. To go deeper, you can join a temple's 'Buddha Seven,' seven straight days of intensive recitation aiming for a state of single-minded focus. When an elder in the family passes away, volunteer recitation groups take turns through the night chanting the Buddha's name to see them off, one of the gentlest farewell rituals in Taiwan.
festivals: The 17th day of the eleventh lunar month is Amitabha Buddha's birthday, when major temples hold 'Buddha Seven' retreats: seven days of intensive recitation aiming for a state of single-minded focus. In addition, the Ullambana services held every seventh lunar month during the Ghost Festival also recite Amitabha's name to help departed souls be reborn in the Pure Land.

name: Kshitigarbha Bodhisattva
domain: Great Vows, Deliverance of Departed Souls, Rescue from Hell
description: 'Until the hells are empty, I will not become a Buddha; only when all beings are saved will I attain enlightenment.' The one who dared to make that vow is Kshitigarbha Bodhisattva, Dizang Wang, honored in folk belief as the Lord of the Netherworld. He is one of the four great bodhisattvas of Chinese Buddhism and stands for the great vow. He is easy to recognize: a monk in a five-leaf Vairocana crown, a ringed staff in one hand to shake open the gates of hell and a luminous pearl in the other to light up the dark realm. In Taiwan his role crosses boundaries: he is a Buddhist bodhisattva, yet he is also woven deep into the Ghost Festival, ancestor worship, and funeral rites. Every seventh lunar month, deliverance services follow one after another at Buddhist temples and Dizang shrines across the island, and when someone in the family dies, inviting monks to chant the Kshitigarbha Sutra and dedicate the merit to the deceased is something many Taiwanese families have experienced. When people want to do something for a loved one who has passed, he is the first one most of them think of.
story:
The Sutra of the Fundamental Vows of Kshitigarbha Bodhisattva records that, countless eons ago, Kshitigarbha was a Brahmin woman. Her mother had slandered the Three Jewels during her life and fell into hell after death. The daughter sold the family's property, made offerings far and wide, and vowed before the Buddha: if my mother can escape the suffering of hell, I will save all beings, and until the hells are empty I will not become a Buddha. Through the power of that vow, she not only freed her mother but set out on the path of rescuing souls in the dark realm. In another life she was a woman named Bright Eyes, who likewise made offerings and vows to the Buddha for a mother fallen into hell. Both stories begin with saving a mother; filial love holds up the weightiest vow in Buddhism.

Legend also says that in the Tang dynasty Kim Gyo-gak, a member of the royal family of Silla (in today's Korea), crossed the sea to Mount Jiuhua in China to practice austerities. After his death his body did not decay and his face looked alive, so he was believed to be a manifestation of Kshitigarbha, and Mount Jiuhua became Kshitigarbha's sacred site, ranked with Putuo, Wutai, and Emei among the four great Buddhist mountains. During the Ming and Qing dynasties, faith in Kshitigarbha crossed the strait with immigrants to Taiwan and fit naturally with the local tradition of caring for the dead. In Taiwan he became a bodhisattva every household knows.

temples.name: Xinzhuang Dizang An
temples.deityStory: Xinzhuang Dizang An (also called Dazhong Temple) is a well-known Kshitigarbha temple in northern Taiwan, dedicated mainly to Kshitigarbha Bodhisattva, the civil and military Dazhong Ye, and Dong Daye. When people lose something, they often pray to Dazhong Ye and Dong Daye for help finding it. The origins of the Guan Jiang Shou performance troupe are also connected with this temple.

temples.name: Tianxiang Xiangde Temple
temples.deityStory: Located at Tianxiang in Taroko, the temple's statue of Kshitigarbha stands tall among the mountains, symbolizing the bodhisattva guarding Taiwan's eastern 'back mountain' region and protecting all beings.

associatedTemples: Xinzhuang Dizang An (Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City)
Manka Dizang Temple (Wanhua District, Taipei City)
Tianxiang Xiangde Temple (Xiulin Township, Hualien County)
worship: Kshitigarbha receives vegetarian offerings: fresh flowers, fruit, clear tea, and cakes. Meat, alcohol, and cigarettes are all taboo. The main text to chant is the Sutra of the Fundamental Vows of Kshitigarbha Bodhisattva, or you can recite his name, 'Namo Dizang Wang Pusa.' What sets this faith apart is doing things on behalf of the dead. When an elder in the family passes away, inviting monks to chant the Kshitigarbha Sutra and dedicate the merit is the most common rite at Taiwanese Buddhist funerals, while the Kshitigarbha services and deliverance rituals held at Dizang shrines and Buddhist temples in the seventh lunar month are for wandering souls with no one to care for them and for generations of ancestors. There is also help for this life: you can light a guangming lamp to pray for safety and wisdom, and some temples fold Tai Sui rites into Kshitigarbha worship as well. If you want to do something for a loved one who has passed, a Dizang temple is the right place to come.
festivals:
**Kshitigarbha Bodhisattva's Birthday**: the 30th day of the seventh lunar month (the 29th in some traditions). Buddhist temples and Dizang temples hold large services with sutra chanting, deliverance rites, and the Flaming Mouth ceremony (a Buddhist rite to feed and deliver hungry ghosts). Because the day falls near the end of the Ghost Festival season, it often carries on directly from the Zhongyuan Pudu rites.

**Zhongyuan Services**: throughout the seventh lunar month (especially around the Zhongyuan Festival on the 15th), Buddhist temples widely hold Kshitigarbha services, the most important religious activity of 'Ghost Month' in Taiwanese Buddhism.

**The Emperor Liang Repentance and the Water and Land Dharma Service**: larger-scale Buddhist deliverance rituals in which Kshitigarbha is one of the central figures, mostly held during the seventh lunar month or at major services.

name: Medicine Buddha
aliases: Medicine Master of Lapis Lazuli Light Tathagata
domain: Healing and Longevity, Removing Misfortune, Wellbeing of Body and Mind
description: Every Lunar New Year, Taiwan's Buddhist temples fill with people lining up to light lamps, most of them Medicine Buddha lamps, asking for a year free of illness and misfortune for their families. The one entrusted with all that health is the Medicine Buddha, in full the Medicine Master of Lapis Lazuli Light Tathagata, also called the Great Physician King Buddha. He presides over the Eastern Pure Land of Lapis Lazuli, and together with Amitabha and Shakyamuni he makes up the 'Buddhas of the Three Directions.' Before becoming a Buddha he made twelve great vows, from 'freedom from illness and peace' to 'fine food and drink' and 'fine clothing,' all aimed squarely at everyday life here and now: a healthy body, a livable life, a settled mind. That is why the Medicine Buddha is the Buddha Taiwanese turn to most when praying for recovery from illness, protection from misfortune, and long life. When someone at home is sick or an elder is getting on in years, lighting a lamp in the Medicine Buddha hall is something many Taiwanese families do every year.
story:
The Sutra of the Merits of the Fundamental Vows of the Medicine Master of Lapis Lazuli Light Tathagata records that countless eons ago, while still a bodhisattva, the Medicine Buddha made twelve great vows, each aimed at the most practical suffering of living beings: chronic illness, lack of food and clothing, unease of body and mind. Once every vow was fulfilled, he became a Buddha and established the Eastern Pure Land of Lapis Lazuli, a Buddha land with no sickness and no want. His attendants on either side are Sunlight Bodhisattva and Moonlight Bodhisattva, and the three together are called the 'Three Sages of the East,' facing the 'Three Sages of the West' of the Western Pure Land from afar: one side receives the dying, the other takes care of this life.

After faith in the Medicine Buddha reached Taiwan, its closeness to this life, to health, family, and livelihood, let it quickly become part of everyday life. Today, every Lunar New Year, from Fo Guang Shan to Dharma Drum Mountain, the lines to light Medicine Buddha lamps and guangming lamps stretch on and on, and many temples combine Tai Sui rites with guangming lamps. You could say that many Taiwanese may never have read the Medicine Buddha Sutra, yet nearly every family has, in one way or another, been looked after by him.
worship: The Medicine Buddha receives vegetarian offerings: fresh flowers, fruit, clear tea, and sweets, with no meat, alcohol, or cigarettes. The main texts are the Medicine Buddha Sutra and the Medicine Buddha mantra, or you can recite his name, 'Namo Xiaozai Yanshou Yaoshi Fo' (Homage to the Medicine Buddha who removes calamity and lengthens life). The most distinctly Taiwanese rite is lighting a Medicine Buddha lamp: every year from Lunar New Year to the Lantern Festival, Buddhist temples open lamp lighting so people can pray for a year of protection and long life for their families, with options from a single person's lamp to a whole family's. People whose year clashes with Tai Sui often take care of their Tai Sui rites at the same time, and large temples such as Fo Guang Shan and Dharma Drum Mountain offer the full service. When someone in the family is ill, pray to the Medicine Buddha and get proper medical care too; treating the illness and praying side by side is old Taiwanese wisdom. Worship does not replace the doctor. It lets the heart settle first.
festivals:
**Medicine Buddha's Birthday**: the 29th day of the ninth lunar month. Buddhist temples hold Medicine Buddha services with chanting of the Medicine Buddha Sutra, life release, and deliverance rites.

**Lunar New Year (Lamp-Lighting Season)**: every year from the 1st day of the first lunar month to the Lantern Festival (the 15th day of the first month) is the traditional time for Taiwanese families to visit Buddhist temples to light Medicine Buddha lamps and perform Tai Sui rites. It is the busiest period of the year for temples.

**Medicine Buddha Seven**: some temples hold a seven-day group retreat called the 'Medicine Buddha Seven,' focused on chanting, reciting the Buddha's name, and dedicating merit, praying for everyone's health of body and mind.

name: Maitreya Buddha
domain: Joy and Ease, The Future Buddha, Tolerance and Generosity
description: Everyone knows the chubby monk at the temple gate, belly bare, laughing so hard his eyes have narrowed to slits. This is Maitreya Buddha, also called Big-Belly Maitreya or the Laughing Buddha, and in folk speech simply Budai, the Cloth-Sack Monk. What many people don't realize is that his official role is the 'Future Buddha.' The sutras foretell that after the teachings of Shakyamuni Buddha have completely died out, Maitreya will be born into the human world, become a Buddha, and save countless beings. Until then he remains Maitreya Bodhisattva, dwelling in the Tushita Heaven and waiting for his time. What Taiwanese love about him is captured in a famous couplet: 'A big belly can hold what the world cannot bear; a ready smile laughs at all the world's absurdities.' However hard life gets, one look at that grin seems to make it bearable. That is why his beaming figure turns up everywhere, from temple gates to shop counters.
story:
Faith in Maitreya comes from the Sutra of Maitreya's Ascent and the Sutra of Maitreya's Descent: Maitreya Bodhisattva now lives in the Tushita Heaven and, in the distant future, will be born among humans and become the next Buddha after Shakyamuni. But the smiling face everyone knows comes from a real person: Qici, the Cloth-Sack Monk of the Later Liang in the Five Dynasties period.

This plump monk wandered from place to place, always grinning, with a big cloth sack slung over his shoulder, telling everyone he met, 'I have a cloth sack, empty as space and free of every hindrance.' No one took him seriously, until, just before he died, he left a verse: 'Maitreya, truly Maitreya, divided into hundreds of billions of bodies, always showing himself to people, yet people never recognize him.' Only then did everyone understand: the chubby monk they had looked down on was an incarnation of Maitreya. From then on, Maitreya statues in China and Taiwan no longer showed the crowned bodhisattva of the Indian scriptures but this smiling monk with his cloth sack. The story leaves a reminder for those who come after: a Buddha may be right beside you, and you just don't recognize him.
worship: To worship Maitreya, just come with a happy heart. Offerings are mainly fresh flowers and fruit; simple is best. Some temples set out candy in front of his statue for visitors to take, symbolizing joy being shared; take one, and remember to leave with a smile. What do people ask him for? A bigger heart, an easygoing outlook, the ability to let go. When work is stuck or something is bottled up inside, look at that big belly and remind yourself to make room. Those who formally practice Maitreya's teachings chant the Sutra of Maitreya's Ascent and vow to be reborn in the Tushita Heaven. Maitreya's birthday is the 1st day of the first lunar month, which is Lunar New Year's Day itself: after ringing the bell for blessings on New Year's Eve, major temples hold his birthday service early on New Year's morning, so the first day of the year begins with learning to smile.
festivals: The 1st day of the first lunar month, Lunar New Year's Day, is Maitreya Buddha's birthday, a sign that the new year should be welcomed with a joyful heart from the very start. After the bell-ringing for blessings on New Year's Eve, major Buddhist temples hold Maitreya's birthday service early on the morning of the 1st, praying for blessings for the year ahead.

name: Manjushri Bodhisattva
domain: Foremost in Wisdom, Studies and Exams, Unhindered Eloquence
description: When exam season arrives, photocopies of admission tickets pile up like small mountains on the altars of temples that honor Manjushri Bodhisattva. Manjushri, also known as Wenshu Shili or Manjushri of Great Wisdom, is the great bodhisattva who is 'foremost in wisdom' in Buddhism. With Samantabhadra Bodhisattva he attends Shakyamuni Buddha, the three together called the 'Shakyamuni Triad'; when the central figure is Vairocana Buddha instead, they are called the 'Three Sages of the Avatamsaka.' His image is unforgettable: his right hand raises the sword of wisdom, which cuts through afflictions rather than enemies; his left holds a Prajna sutra; and he rides a blue-green lion, symbol of wisdom's fierce power. In Taiwan he is the guardian of students and test-takers, and visiting Manjushri before a big exam to ask for wisdom and a place on the list of successful candidates is a fixed routine for many families. But Manjushri is about more than exams. What he gives is the ability to think things through, so you can bring life's hard questions to him too.
story:
Manjushri holds an astonishingly high place in the sutras. In the Avatamsaka Sutra he is the first teacher of the youth Sudhana and his fifty-three visits, the one whose words send the boy on a quest to seek out wise teachers. The Vimalakirti Sutra is even more vivid. The layman Vimalakirti fell ill, and the Buddha asked his disciples to visit him, but one after another they declined, because Vimalakirti's eloquence was so sharp that anyone who went would be left speechless. In the end only Manjushri accepted the task, and the meeting of these two supreme minds produced the most brilliant exchange on the Dharma in all the sutras.

The scriptures also record a secret: Manjushri actually became a Buddha long ago. In the past he was the Buddha called Supreme King of the Dragon Lineage, and in the future he will be the Tathagata Universal Vision. He took the form of a bodhisattva again only in order to help living beings. Mount Wutai in China is revered as Manjushri's sacred site, and eminent monks through the ages have made pilgrimages there. This faith in wisdom came to Taiwan with Buddhism and became the firmest support of Taiwan's test-takers.

temples.name: Jinshan Ciyin Temple
temples.deityStory: Dedicated to Manjushri Bodhisattva, the temple often sees students bringing photocopies of their exam admission tickets to pray. According to the temple, it is the largest Manjushri place of practice in northern Taiwan.

associatedTemples: Jinshan Ciyin Temple (Jinshan District, New Taipei City)
worship: Offerings to Manjushri have one special feature: besides fresh flowers and fruit, you can offer stationery, pens and books alike. What test-takers do most often is bring a copy of their admission ticket or the pen they will use in the exam to the altar to be blessed, praying for a clear mind in the exam room and a place on the list of successful candidates. Those who practice Manjushri's teachings recite his heart mantra, 'Om A Ra Pa Ca Na Dhih,' or chant the Prajnaparamita Sutra Spoken by Manjushri. On his birthday, the 4th day of the fourth lunar month, temples hold wisdom services, and around exam season many temples also offer wisdom lamps you can light. One reminder: Manjushri gives wisdom, not answers. You still have to study; his blessing is that what you study sinks in.
festivals: The 4th day of the fourth lunar month is Manjushri Bodhisattva's birthday, when major Buddhist temples hold wisdom services and prayer events. Many temples near schools also hold 'Wisdom Lamp services' timed to exam season, so students can light lamps and pray for blessings.

name: Samantabhadra Bodhisattva
domain: The Power of Great Vows in Action, Putting Practice into Action, Upholding the Dharma
description: Each of Buddhism's four great bodhisattvas has a specialty: Guanyin stands for compassion, Manjushri for wisdom, Kshitigarbha for vows, and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, also called the Bodhisattva of Universal Auspiciousness or Samantabhadra of Great Practice, stands for practice: actually putting the Dharma into action. In the Avatamsaka Sutra he is honored as the 'eldest son of all Buddhas,' and with Manjushri on the other side he attends Shakyamuni Buddha, the three forming the 'Shakyamuni Triad.' Manjushri stands for seeing clearly, Samantabhadra for getting it done. He is easy to recognize, riding a white elephant with six tusks. The six tusks stand for the six perfections: generosity, moral discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom. In Taiwan, faith in Samantabhadra is not as widespread as faith in Guanyin or Kshitigarbha, but his 'Ten Great Vows' serve as a guide to action in the morning and evening services of countless Buddhists. Those who know understand: to honor Samantabhadra is to honor the idea of not just talking but doing.
story:
The grand finale of the Avatamsaka Sutra belongs to Samantabhadra. In the chapter 'Entering the Dharma Realm,' the youth Sudhana visits 53 wise teachers one after another, meeting Guanyin and Maitreya along the way, and only when he finally reaches Samantabhadra does he attain completion. The end of the quest is not some deeper theory but simply doing. Legend says that countless eons ago Samantabhadra made a great vow to help all beings attain Buddhahood through great practice. His Ten Great Vows, from paying homage to all Buddhas and repenting of karmic obstacles to always following the needs of beings and dedicating all merit universally, break practice down into ten achievable actions.

The six-tusked white elephant he rides comes from Indian tradition and symbolizes nobility, purity, and steady strength: every step an elephant takes is firmly planted, just like practice. Mount Emei in Sichuan has long been Samantabhadra's sacred site, ranked with Putuo, Wutai, and Jiuhua among the four great Buddhist mountains. During the Sui and Tang dynasties, eminent monks of the Tiantai and Huayan schools placed special weight on the teaching of his Ten Great Vows, and in the Ming and Qing dynasties the faith came to Taiwan with Buddhism, where it continues today.
worship: Samantabhadra receives vegetarian offerings: fresh flowers, fruit, and clear tea, with no meat, alcohol, or cigarettes. The first choice of text is the 'Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra' chapter of the Avatamsaka Sutra, or you can recite his name, 'Namo Daxing Puxian Pusa' (Homage to Samantabhadra of Great Practice). But the real focus of this faith is not on the altar but off it. The Ten Great Vows are meant to be lived: paying homage to the Buddhas every day, rejoicing when you see others do good, honestly repenting when you go wrong, and dedicating your merit to all beings. Many Buddhists treat the ten vows as a daily practice checklist and carry them out one by one. What do people ask him for? The ability to follow through, and vows that never weaken. If your plans always stall at step one, this action-minded bodhisattva is an especially good teacher. On his birthday, the 21st day of the second lunar month, temples hold sutra-chanting services.
festivals:
**Samantabhadra Bodhisattva's Birthday**: the 21st day of the second lunar month. Buddhist temples celebrate the day with chanting of the 'Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra' chapter of the Avatamsaka Sutra, Dharma talks, and other rites.

**Avatamsaka Services**: some temples (especially those of the Huayan tradition) hold an annual 'Avatamsaka Service' lasting from several days to a month, chanting the entire Avatamsaka Sutra, with Samantabhadra as a central figure.

name: Skanda Bodhisattva
domain: Dharma Protector, Guardian of Monasteries, Driving Out Evil
description: Step into a Buddhist temple in Taiwan and the first figure you meet is the smiling Maitreya. Turn around, though, and there stands a warrior in golden armor holding a vajra club, facing the main hall. This is Skanda (Weituo) Bodhisattva, also called Weituo Tian or General Wei, the best-known Dharma protector in Chinese Buddhism. Maitreya faces outward to greet guests, Skanda faces inward to guard; 'Maitreya when you enter, Skanda when you look back' is the traditional layout of the Hall of Heavenly Kings. His duties are to protect the Dharma, guard the monastery, and subdue demonic forces. Those in the know look at one more detail: how Skanda holds his vajra club tells you the monastery's rules for visiting monks. Laid across both arms, it welcomes a wandering monk to stay for three days; held upright at the waist, it offers a one-day stay; planted on the ground, it means no lodging is available. Next time you pass through a temple gate, remember to look back at this silent guardian general.
story:
Skanda's most famous legend is 'the swift ghost who stole the Buddha's tooth.' It is said that after the Buddha's nirvana, the heavenly beings gathered beneath the twin sala trees to receive his tooth relic. In a moment when everyone was lost in grief and off guard, a swift-footed ghost darted in, snatched the tooth, and ran. The moment Skanda heard, he threw on his golden armor, seized his club, and gave chase. No matter how fast or how far the ghost fled, he stayed right on its heels, until at last he took the tooth back and returned it to the stupa. From then on he was honored as a Dharma protector: whenever the true Dharma is threatened, he will pursue to the very end.

Another account links Skanda to the Indian war god Kumara, originally a many-faced, many-armed deity who rode a peacock. As Buddhism spread east, he was transformed into a Chinese general, refined yet formidable, and in the Ming and Qing dynasties he crossed the sea to Taiwan with Buddhism. Today, behind the gates of Taiwan's Buddhist temples, this general who has kept up his chase for a thousand years still stands guard.
worship: Skanda is a protector of the monastery, not the place to bring personal wishes. Devotees rarely ask him for wealth or romance; most pray for diligence in their Buddhist study, steady progress in practice, and the protection of the Dharma. Offerings are mainly vegetarian; you can light a pure lamp and chant the Heart Sutra or Skanda's mantra. Before taking refuge or receiving precepts, Buddhists often pay their respects to Skanda first, expressing a wish to be guided and protected by the Dharma. When you visit major monasteries such as Fo Guang Shan, Dharma Drum Mountain, or Chung Tai Chan Monastery, don't forget to pause in the Hall of Heavenly Kings and see how Skanda holds his vajra club. It is the monastery's silent notice to wandering monks, and one of the most interesting things to look for in a Taiwanese Buddhist temple.
festivals:
**Skanda Bodhisattva's Birthday**: the 3rd day of the sixth lunar month. Buddhist temples celebrate with sutra chanting, recitation of the Praise of Skanda Bodhisattva, life release, and other rites.

**Buddha's Birthday (8th day of the fourth lunar month)**: during the Bathing the Buddha Festival, Skanda is also honored as the Buddha's Dharma protector, and some temples add his mantra to the Bathing the Buddha service.

**Monastery Founding and Consecration Rites**: whenever a monastery is newly built, rebuilt, or consecrated, Skanda is one of the figures who must be honored, as a prayer for his protection in the years ahead.

name: Sangharama Bodhisattva
domain: Dharma Protector, Guardian of the Monastery, Symbol of Loyalty and Righteousness
description: You may not know it, but Lord Guan goes by another name inside Buddhist temples. Sangharama Bodhisattva, also called the Venerable Sangharama, is the guardian deity of monasteries in Chinese Buddhism, and his most famous manifestation is none other than Guan Yu, the Holy Emperor Guan. 'Sangharama' originally means the pure grounds where a community of monks lives, and Sangharama Bodhisattva is the guardian of those grounds. Legend says that after Guan Yu died in battle, he was converted by Master Zhiyi of the Tiantai school, took refuge in Buddhism, and from then on guarded Buddhist monasteries as a Dharma protector. In Chinese Buddhist temples he is placed symmetrically with Skanda, one inside and one outside: 'outside, Skanda subdues demons; inside, Sangharama guards the monastery.' And so in Taiwan the same Lord Guan has a double identity: in a Guandi temple he is the god of war and a god of wealth, while in a Buddhist temple's Sangharama hall he is a protector of the Dharma.
story:
Legend says that at the end of the Eastern Han dynasty, Guan Yu was defeated at Maicheng and beheaded by the state of Wu, but his spirit would not disperse and often appeared around Jingzhou. One night it drifted to Mount Yuquan in Hubei, where Master Zhiyi of the Tiantai school was practicing in the mountains, and demanded fiercely, 'Give me back my head!' The master calmly replied, 'General, in your life you killed countless people. From whom should they demand back their heads?' The words struck like thunder. Guan Yu suddenly realized how heavy his karma of killing was, repented on the spot, took refuge, and received the precepts to become a protector of Buddhism, Sangharama Bodhisattva, appearing at Mount Yuquan to protect the Dharma.

The earliest record of this story is Dong Ting's 'Record of the Restoration of the Guan Shrine at Yuquan,' written in the 18th year of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty (802 AD); the full account of the conversion appears in Northern Song sources. The dates don't match history (Master Zhiyi was born more than three hundred years after Guan Yu), yet it is one of the most graceful strokes in the Sinicization of Buddhism: inviting the warrior saint the Chinese revered most into the Buddhist fold as its guardian. In the Ming and Qing dynasties, this faith crossed the sea with immigrants to Taiwan, giving rise to Taiwan's distinctive scene of 'one deity with two names, worshipped by both Buddhists and Taoists.'
worship: Worshipping Sangharama follows the rules of the Buddhist temple: vegetarian offerings, chanting the Heart Sutra and the Great Compassion Mantra, or reciting his name, 'Namo Qielan Shengzhong Pusa' (Homage to the Holy Sangharama Bodhisattvas). He is a protector of the monastery, so devotees mostly pray for smooth progress in practice and a flourishing monastery, and seldom bring personal worldly matters. Interestingly, change the setting and the way of worship changes too. The same Lord Guan is, in a Guandi temple, the god of war, a god of wealth, and a god of loyalty, someone you can ask for help with your career or your finances; in a Buddhist temple's Sangharama hall he is a Dharma protector, and what you ask for is the protection of the Dharma. Before you decide what to pray for, look at which kind of temple you have walked into. That is where Taiwanese faith is at its most flexible. On his birthday, the 13th day of the fifth lunar month, Buddhist temples and Guandi temples often celebrate on the same day, with both Buddhists and Taoists joining in.
festivals:
**Sangharama Bodhisattva's Birthday**: the 13th day of the fifth lunar month (the 24th day of the sixth lunar month in some traditions). This is also the day popularly known as the birthday of the Holy Emperor Guan, and both Buddhist temples and Guandi temples hold celebrations.

**Sangharama Services at Buddhist Temples**: on the birthday, Buddhist temples chant the Praise of Sangharama Bodhisattva, hold Dharma services, and dedicate merit to the Dharma protectors.

**Integration with Lord Guan Worship**: because Sangharama Bodhisattva and the Holy Emperor Guan are the same deity, many temples in Taiwan celebrate Sangharama's birthday and Lord Guan's birthday together, with processions, sutra chanting, and other activities, a distinctively Taiwanese expression of **combined Buddhist and Taoist festivals**.

name: Acala (Fudo Myoo)
domain: Subduing Demons and Removing Obstacles, Steadfast Will, Protecting Spiritual Practice
description: Deep blue skin, glaring eyes, flames roaring behind him: people seeing Acala (Fudo Myoo) for the first time are often startled. How can a Buddhist protector look like this? Acala, also called Fudo-son, the Immovable Lord, is the foremost of the Five Great Wisdom Kings of Esoteric Buddhism. A 'Wisdom King' is neither a Buddha nor a bodhisattva but the wrathful form the Buddhas take on to subdue stubborn beings who are hard to reach, and Acala is a manifestation of Mahavairocana. In his right hand is a demon-subduing sword that cuts through afflictions, in his left a lasso that draws beings out of suffering, and his feet rest on a solid rock, a sign of resolve that never retreats. The fire burns not people but karmic obstacles. Faith in Acala took a particular route into Taiwan: it came mainly through Japanese Buddhism (such as the Shingon school) during the Japanese colonial era, not through Chinese Buddhism, and the Acala grotto in the Beitou hot spring district is a relic left from the Taisho era of Japanese rule. A niche faith, but one with a deep story.
story:
In Esoteric Buddhist teaching, when Mahavairocana faces beings who cannot be moved even by a kind face, he changes his face, appearing as the wrathful Acala. That wrath is not real anger but compassion as thunder: some people are sunk so deep that they need to be shaken awake. The heart of his name is 'immovable.' It does not mean standing still; it means a mind unmoved by outside circumstances. Faced with the greatest temptation, fear, or suffering, the resolve to practice stays solid as rock and does not give up a single step.

In the Tang dynasty, the Three Great Masters of the Kaiyuan era, Shubhakarasimha, Vajrabodhi, and Amoghavajra, brought Esoteric teachings to China, and the Japanese master Kukai (Kobo Daishi) later carried them back to Japan and founded the Shingon school. From then on Acala became one of the most revered protectors in Japan, especially as a steadfast support for mountain ascetics (Shugendo) facing danger and inner demons. During the Japanese colonial era this faith crossed the sea to Taiwan and left its mark around Taipei and Keelung; Beitou's Puji Temple is a Japanese-style Buddhist temple preserved to this day. After the war, Chinese Buddhism became the mainstream, but Acala did not disappear. He still stands quietly in Esoteric practice circles, like the rock beneath his feet.

temples.name: Beitou Acala Grotto
temples.deityStory: A grotto carved into the cliff beside a waterfall, containing a stone relief of Acala. It was built during the Taisho era of Japanese rule, funded by Sano Shotaro, who ran the Hoshinoyu hot spring inn.

temples.name: Guanziling Huowangye Temple
temples.deityStory: In the early years of Japanese rule, the Japanese set up an image of Acala at the source of the Guanziling hot springs. Later, residents pooled money to build a temple and recreate the statue, renaming him Huowangye, the Fire King. The temple is the center of faith for the hot spring businesses and residents.

associatedTemples: Beitou Acala Grotto (Beitou District, Taipei City)
Guanziling Huowangye Temple (Baihe District, Tainan City)
worship: There are two ways to worship Acala in Taiwan. In Chinese Buddhist settings, offerings are vegetarian and devotees recite Acala's heart mantra, a practice common among lay practitioners of Esoteric teachings. The most distinctive practice in Japanese-style Esoteric settings is the goma fire offering: wishes are written on goma sticks and thrown into the fire altar to burn, symbolizing the flames consuming karmic obstacles and carrying one's vows up to the Buddhas. Complete goma rites are uncommon in Taiwan and are mostly seen only at large Esoteric services. What do people ask him for? Acala is about holding on. When your will is weak, when obstacles make you want to give up, when you need to cut off a bad habit, he is especially fitting to pray to for steadfast resolve and unwavering practice. Japanese tradition treats the 28th of every month as Acala's day, and some practitioners in Taiwan still keep this day by reciting mantras and sitting in meditation.
festivals:
**Acala's Day**: Japanese temples hold Acala services on the 28th of every month.

**Goma Services**: Acala's most representative rite is the goma fire offering, usually held on his feast day, during the New Year period, or when a practitioner makes a special vow.

**Shugendo-Related Practice**: some Taiwanese practitioners influenced by Japanese Buddhism still keep the tradition of a monthly Acala gathering (on the 28th of each month), practicing through mantra recitation, sitting meditation, and goma.

A note: faith in Acala remains niche in Taiwan, mainly among **people interested in Esoteric Buddhism and students of Japanese-style Buddhism**. Ordinary visitors can observe its cultural traces at the few temples more deeply influenced by the Japanese colonial era.
